tips.title: Denatured, never killed
tips.body: An enzyme is a **protein**, not a living thing, so it cannot be **killed**. Heat or the wrong pH **changes the shape of the active site**, so the substrate no longer fits. The word is **denatured**, and using *killed* loses the mark even when the biology behind it is right.

tips.title: Cold does not denature
tips.body: Below the optimum an enzyme is **slow**, not **denatured**. The particles have **less kinetic energy**, so there are **fewer collisions** — warm it up again and the rate comes back. **Denaturing is permanent**, and it is caused by **high** temperature or **extreme** pH.

tips.title: Rate is one over time
tips.body: When a question times how long a reaction takes, the **rate** is $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$, usually written as $\dfrac{1000}{\text{time in seconds}}$ to avoid tiny decimals. **Twice the time means half the rate** — a quick check that you have not accidentally plotted time instead.

tips.title: Three enzymes, three products
tips.body: **Carbohydrase** breaks carbohydrates into **sugars**. **Protease** breaks proteins into **amino acids**. **Lipase** breaks lipids into **fatty acids and glycerol** — the only one with **two** products, and the one most often left half-written.

tips.title: Levelling off means saturated
tips.body: A substrate-concentration graph that rises then **levels off** has run out of **active sites**, not out of substrate. Every site is occupied, so adding more substrate changes nothing: the **enzyme concentration** has become the limiting factor.

why.matters:
The reactions that keep you alive would take years at body temperature, and a cell cannot solve that by getting hotter. **Enzymes** are the answer: each one makes a single reaction fast, at 37 °C, and leaves everything else alone.

That specificity comes from **shape** — the substrate fits the active site and nothing else does. Which is also the weakness: anything that changes the shape, heat or the wrong pH, stops the enzyme permanently. Nearly every question here is one of those two consequences of a shape.

examples.title: Why a very high fever is dangerous
examples.body:
Human enzymes work fastest at about **37 °C**, and a mild fever is useful: it speeds up the immune response and makes life harder for the pathogen.

At temperatures well above body temperature the curve does not just flatten — it falls off a cliff, because enzymes begin to **denature** and the active site loses its shape. And that is **permanent**: cooling down does not put it back. A cold body is slow and recoverable; an overheated one is damaged, which is why the two ends of the graph are not mirror images.

visual.alt: A curve of enzyme activity against temperature that rises gently to a peak at thirty-seven degrees Celsius and then falls away steeply as the enzyme denatures

examples.title: Why jelly will not set with fresh pineapple
examples.body:
Put fresh pineapple in a jelly and it stays liquid. Use tinned pineapple and it sets perfectly. The difference is an enzyme.

Jelly sets because gelatine is a **protein** whose long molecules tangle. Fresh pineapple contains a **protease**, which breaks proteins into amino acids, so the gelatine is taken apart faster than it can set. Tinned pineapple was heated during canning, which **denatured** the enzyme — and since denaturing is permanent, cooling the tin back down does not bring it back. It is the same protease that makes pineapple juice sting your mouth.

visual.alt: A table of fresh, tinned and boiled pineapple in jelly: the protease in fresh pineapple digests the gelatine so the jelly never sets, while heating the fruit denatures the enzyme and the jelly sets

examples.title: Why your stomach and your mouth need different enzymes
examples.body:
**Starch** digestion starts in the mouth, stops in the stomach and starts again in the small intestine — and the same enzyme cannot work in all three, because the pH is completely different.

**Amylase** in the mouth has an optimum near **pH 7**. The stomach is around **pH 2**, acidic enough to kill most pathogens, and amylase denatures there; **pepsin** is the protease built for those conditions. Each enzyme is shaped for one place in the body, which is why the body needs so many of them.

visual.alt: A table of two enzymes and where each works: pepsin in the stomach at about pH two, and amylase in the mouth at about pH seven, each shaped for its own conditions

steps.title: What an enzyme is, and the active site
steps.body:
**Enzymes are biological catalysts.** A catalyst **speeds up a reaction without being used up**, so one enzyme molecule works over and over again.

An enzyme is a **protein**, folded into a particular **three-dimensional shape**. Somewhere on that shape is a pocket called the **active site**, and that is where the reaction happens.

**The mechanism, in the order the spec asks for:**

1. The **substrate** — the molecule the enzyme works on — collides with the enzyme.
2. It fits into the **active site**, because the two shapes are **complementary**.
3. The reaction happens, and the **products** leave.
4. The enzyme is **unchanged**, and takes another substrate.

**Specificity is the consequence of the shape.** Each enzyme has an active site of a particular shape, so **only a substrate with a complementary shape fits**. This is why **one enzyme catalyses one reaction**, and it is described as the **lock and key** model: the wrong key does not turn the lock, however hard you push.

**So every explanation in this topic runs through shape.** Why is an enzyme specific? Shape. Why does heat stop it working? Shape. Getting into the habit of naming the **active site** in the answer is most of the skill.

steps.title: Denaturing
steps.body:
**If the shape of the active site changes, the substrate no longer fits.** That is denaturing, and it is the whole of spec point 1.8.

**What causes it:**

- **Temperatures above the optimum.** The heat makes the protein **vibrate** so much that the bonds holding its folded shape **break**.
- **pH values away from the optimum.** The wrong pH also breaks those bonds.

**What happens next:** the **active site changes shape**, the substrate is **no longer complementary**, so it **cannot bind**, and the reaction **stops**.

**Two things to be careful about.**

**An enzyme is not alive**, so it cannot be **killed**. It is a protein. The word is **denatured**, and examiners mark it strictly because *killed* suggests a misunderstanding of what an enzyme is.

**Cold does not denature.** Below the optimum the molecules have **less kinetic energy**, so they **collide less often and with less energy** — the reaction is **slow**, but the enzyme is **undamaged**. Warm it back up and the rate returns. **Denaturing is permanent**; being cold is not.

That difference is the single most reliable question in this topic: *explain why the rate is low at 5 °C and at 70 °C*. The two answers are **completely different**, and an answer that gives denaturing for both throws away half the marks.

steps.title: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration
steps.body:
**Three factors, and the spec asks for the effect of each.** Two make the same shape of graph and one does not.

**Temperature.** The rate **rises** as temperature increases, because the molecules have **more kinetic energy**, so there are **more frequent collisions with more energy**. It reaches a **peak at the optimum** — about **37 °C** for human enzymes — and then **falls steeply**, because above the optimum the enzyme **denatures**.

**Notice the graph is not symmetrical.** The rise is gradual and the fall is sharp, because denaturing happens quickly once it begins. A sketch with a symmetrical hill has missed that.

**pH.** The same shape: a **peak at the optimum pH**, falling away on **both** sides, because a pH away from the optimum also **changes the shape of the active site**. Different enzymes have different optima — **pepsin** works in the stomach at about **pH 2**, while **amylase** works at about **pH 7**. So *the optimum pH is 7* is only true for some enzymes.

**Substrate concentration.** A different shape. The rate **rises** as substrate is added, then **levels off**. It levels off because **every active site is occupied** — the enzyme is **saturated**. Adding more substrate cannot help, because there is nothing free to bind to; the **enzyme concentration** has become the limiting factor.

**That distinction is worth holding.** A levelling-off graph means *something has run out*, and here it is **active sites**, not substrate.

steps.title: Core practical 1.10: the effect of pH on enzyme activity
steps.body:
**This is core practical 1.10.** The usual version uses **amylase**, which breaks down **starch**.

**The method:**

1. Put a drop of **iodine solution** in each well of a **spotting tile**.
2. Heat a **beaker of water** with a **Bunsen burner** to a set temperature, such as 35 °C, checking it with a thermometer. Stand the tubes of **amylase**, **buffer** and **starch** in it for a few minutes so that they all reach that temperature before they are mixed, and keep the reaction tube in it.
3. Mix **amylase** with a **buffer solution** at a known pH. A buffer holds the pH steady while the reaction runs.
4. Add **starch** solution and start the **stopwatch**.
5. Every **10 seconds**, take a drop of the mixture and add it to a well of iodine.
6. While **starch is present** the iodine turns **blue-black**. When the starch is **all digested**, the iodine stays **orange-brown**. Record that **time**.
7. Repeat at **different pH values**, keeping temperature, enzyme concentration, starch concentration and volumes the **same**.

**What the results mean.** The **shorter** the time, the **faster** the enzyme is working. So the **rate** is $\dfrac{1000}{\text{time in seconds}}$, and the pH giving the **shortest time** is the **optimum**.

**Why iodine.** It is an **indicator for starch** — and here it is used to detect the **disappearance** of the substrate rather than the appearance of a product. A question asking *what is the dependent variable?* is answered by the **time for the starch to disappear**, not by the colour.

**The control variables matter.** Temperature especially: if it drifts, the comparison between pH values means nothing, which is why the tubes stand in a beaker of water heated by a Bunsen burner, with the thermometer checked throughout.

steps.title: Rate calculations
steps.body:
**Spec point 1.11 asks for rate calculations**, and they come in two forms.

When the question gives a **time for the reaction to finish**, use $\text{rate} = \dfrac{1000}{\text{time in seconds}}$.

When it gives an **amount of product made in a time**, use $\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{time}}$.

Both are the same idea: how much happens per unit of time.

steps.title: What enzymes build and break down
steps.body:
**Spec point 1.12 has two halves, and most people learn only one.** Enzymes catalyse both the **breakdown** of large molecules and the **synthesis** of them.

**Breaking down** — the three to know:

- **Carbohydrase** breaks **carbohydrates** into **sugars**. **Amylase** is the example: it breaks **starch** into sugars.
- **Protease** breaks **proteins** into **amino acids**.
- **Lipase** breaks **lipids** into **fatty acids and glycerol**.

**Lipase is the one to be careful with**: its products are **two** things, and an answer giving only *fatty acids* has given half of it.

**Building up.** The same three families of molecules are also **made** by enzymes: sugars are joined into **carbohydrates**, amino acids into **proteins**, and fatty acids and glycerol into **lipids**. The spec says *synthesis of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids* **and** their breakdown, so a question can ask about either direction.

**Why breaking down matters in digestion.** Large molecules are **insoluble** and **cannot be absorbed** through the wall of the small intestine. Breaking them into small, **soluble** molecules is what makes absorption possible. That is the reason digestion needs enzymes at all.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Low and high temperatures fail for completely different reasons.** Below the optimum: **less kinetic energy**, so **fewer successful collisions** between enzyme and substrate — the enzyme is **undamaged** and warming restores the rate. Above the optimum: the bonds holding the protein's shape **break**, the **active site changes shape**, the substrate is **no longer complementary**, and the change is **permanent**. A question asking about both is testing exactly whether you know they are not the same, and giving denaturing twice discards half the marks.

**Never write that an enzyme was killed.** An enzyme is a **protein**. It is **denatured**. This is marked strictly, and rightly, because the wrong word signals a wrong model of what an enzyme is.

**Say which shape changed.** The strongest denaturing answers name the **active site** specifically, and give the chain: bonds break → the active site changes shape → the substrate no longer **fits** → no **enzyme-substrate complex** forms → the reaction stops. Each link is a mark.

**Levelling off is about active sites, not substrate.** When a rate-against-substrate graph flattens, every **active site is occupied** and the enzyme is **saturated**. The limiting factor is now the **enzyme concentration** — so the way to raise the rate is to add **more enzyme**, not more substrate. Being able to say what would raise it is what separates a grade 9 answer.

**Optimum pH is not always 7.** **Pepsin** works in the stomach at about **pH 2** and would be denatured at pH 7; **amylase** works at about **pH 7**. An enzyme's optimum matches **where in the body it works**, which is a better thing to know than any single number.

**Use rate, not time, when you compare.** A **longer** time means a **slower** reaction, so raw times run the opposite way to the thing you are describing. Converting to $\dfrac{1000}{\text{time}}$ makes higher mean faster, and gives a free check: **doubling the time must halve the rate**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Enzymes are biological catalysts**: they **speed up a reaction without being used up**.
- An enzyme is a **protein** with a specific shape, and the **active site** is where the **substrate** binds.
- Only a substrate whose shape is **complementary** fits, so each enzyme is **specific** — the **lock and key** model.
- **Denaturing**: high temperature or extreme pH **breaks bonds**, the **active site changes shape**, and the substrate **no longer fits**.
- An enzyme is **denatured**, never **killed** — it is not alive.
- **Below the optimum** the enzyme is **slow, not damaged**: less **kinetic energy**, so fewer collisions. Warming restores the rate.
- **Temperature**: rate rises to an **optimum** (about **37 °C** in humans), then falls **steeply**.
- **pH**: a peak at the **optimum pH**, falling on both sides. **Pepsin** about **pH 2**, **amylase** about **pH 7**.
- **Substrate concentration**: rate rises then **levels off**, because all **active sites are occupied** — the enzyme is **saturated**.
- Once saturated, the limiting factor is the **enzyme concentration**, so adding **more enzyme** raises the rate.
- **Core practical 1.10**: amylase, starch and a **buffer**; sample into **iodine** every 10 s; the end is when the iodine stays **orange-brown**.
- $\text{rate} = \dfrac{1000}{\text{time in seconds}}$, or $\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{time}}$ when an amount is given.
- **Carbohydrase** → **sugars**. **Protease** → **amino acids**. **Lipase** → **fatty acids and glycerol**.
- Enzymes catalyse **synthesis** as well as **breakdown**, and the spec asks for both.
- Breaking large molecules down matters because they are **insoluble** and **cannot be absorbed** until they are small.

questions.prompt: At pH 7 starch was digested in 20 s; at pH 5 it took 60 s. A student says the reaction at pH 5 was faster, because 60 is the bigger number. Calculate how many times faster the reaction at pH 7 actually was.
questions.solution: The student has it the wrong way round: a **longer** time is a **slower** reaction. questions.prompt: A student measures the rate of an enzyme reaction at 5 °C, 37 °C and 70 °C, and finds the rate is low at 5 °C, highest at 37 °C, and almost zero at 70 °C. Explain these results.
questions.solution:
At **5 °C** the rate is low because the molecules have **little kinetic energy**. Enzyme and substrate therefore **collide less often**, and with less energy when they do, so fewer substrate molecules enter the active site in a given time. Nothing has gone wrong with the enzyme itself: the bonds holding its shape are **intact**, and if the mixture were warmed to 37 °C the rate would **return**. Low temperature slows an enzyme; it does not damage it.

At **37 °C** the rate is highest. This is the **optimum** for human enzymes, and it is a balance: there is now enough kinetic energy for **frequent, successful collisions**, while the temperature is still low enough that the enzyme's **shape is undamaged**.

At **70 °C** the rate is almost zero, and the reason is completely different from the reason at 5 °C. Above the optimum, the heat makes the protein **vibrate** so violently that the **bonds holding its folded shape break**. The **active site changes shape**, so the substrate is **no longer complementary** to it and **cannot bind** — no enzyme-substrate complex forms, and the reaction stops. The enzyme is **denatured**, and unlike the cold this change is **permanent**: cooling the mixture back to 37 °C would not restore the rate.

It is worth being exact about the word. An enzyme is a **protein**, not a living thing, so it is never **killed** — it is **denatured**. And the shape that matters is specifically the **active site**: saying only that the enzyme changed shape leaves out the step that explains why the reaction stops.

States that at 5 °C the enzyme is not damaged, and the rate would return on warming.
At 37 °C: the optimum, where collisions are frequent enough but the enzyme is still intact.
At 70 °C: bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site changes shape, the substrate is no longer complementary and cannot bind.

questions.modelAnswer:
At **5 °C** the rate is low because the molecules have **little kinetic energy**. Enzyme and substrate therefore **collide less often**, and with less energy when they do, so fewer substrate molecules enter the active site in a given time. Nothing has gone wrong with the enzyme itself: the bonds holding its shape are **intact**, and if the mixture were warmed to 37 °C the rate would **return**. Low temperature slows an enzyme; it does not damage it.

At **37 °C** the rate is highest. This is the **optimum** for human enzymes, and it is a balance: there is now enough kinetic energy for **frequent, successful collisions**, while the temperature is still low enough that the enzyme's **shape is undamaged**.

At **70 °C** the rate is almost zero, and the reason is completely different from the reason at 5 °C. Above the optimum, the heat makes the protein **vibrate** so violently that the **bonds holding its folded shape break**. The **active site changes shape**, so the substrate is **no longer complementary** to it and **cannot bind** — no enzyme-substrate complex forms, and the reaction stops. The enzyme is **denatured**, and unlike the cold this change is **permanent**: cooling the mixture back to 37 °C would not restore the rate.

It is worth being exact about the word. An enzyme is a **protein**, not a living thing, so it is never **killed** — it is **denatured**. And the shape that matters is specifically the **active site**: saying only that the enzyme changed shape leaves out the step that explains why the reaction stops.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase, and explain how you would use the results to find the optimum pH.
questions.solution:
I would put a drop of **iodine solution** into each well of a **spotting tile**, and heat a **beaker of water** with a **Bunsen burner** to a set temperature, checked with a thermometer. I would stand the tubes of amylase, buffer and starch in it for a few minutes so that they reach that temperature. In a test tube I would mix **amylase** with a **buffer solution** of a known **pH** — the buffer holds the pH **steady** while the reaction runs, so the value being tested is the value actually acting. I would then add **starch** solution and start a **stopwatch**.

Every **10 seconds** I would take a drop of the mixture with a pipette and add it to the next well of iodine. While starch is still present the iodine turns **blue-black**. When the starch has been **completely digested**, the iodine **stays orange-brown**, and I would record the **time** at which that first happens. That time is the **dependent variable**.

The **independent variable** is the **pH**, which I would change by using buffers at pH 3, 5, 7, 9 and so on. Several things must be kept the **same** or the comparison means nothing: the **temperature**, held by the beaker of water, the **concentration of amylase**, the **concentration of starch**, and the **volumes** used. Temperature matters most, because it affects enzyme activity as strongly as pH does, and a drift in it would be indistinguishable from the effect I am trying to measure.

To interpret the results I would convert each time into a **rate**, using $\text{rate} = \dfrac{1000}{\text{time in seconds}}$. This matters because a **longer** time means a **slower** reaction, so raw times run in the opposite direction to the quantity I am describing; converting them makes a **higher number mean a faster enzyme**. Plotting rate against pH gives a curve with a **peak**, and the pH at that peak is the **optimum**. It also gives a free check: if one pH took **twice** as long as another, its rate should be exactly **half**.

questions.prompt: Enzymes catalyse the synthesis of large molecules as well as their breakdown. Which of these is a synthesis reaction?
questions.solution: **Amino acids joined to make a protein** is synthesis: small molecules built into a large one. The other three are breakdown, the direction used in digestion. Enzymes also join sugars into carbohydrates, and fatty acids and glycerol into lipids.

examTechnique.body:
Almost every enzyme question is answered through the **shape of the active site**, so make that the spine of the answer. Specificity: only a **complementary** substrate fits. Denaturing: the **active site changes shape**, so the substrate **no longer fits**. Saturation: every **active site is occupied**.

The second thing to watch is the **direction** of the quantity you are given. Reaction **times** run the opposite way to **rates** — a longer time is a slower reaction — so convert before comparing, and the arithmetic will check itself.
examinerErrors: Writing that an enzyme is **killed**. It is a **protein**, and the word is **denatured**.
Saying that a **low temperature denatures** the enzyme. Cold gives **fewer collisions**, and the effect is **reversible**.
Saying only that the **enzyme** changes shape, rather than the **active site**.
Explaining a levelling-off graph as the **substrate running out**, when it is the **active sites** that are all occupied.
Stating that the optimum pH is **7 for all enzymes** — **pepsin** works at about **pH 2**.
Giving only **fatty acids** as the product of lipase, and omitting **glycerol**.
Comparing raw **times** as if a bigger number meant a faster reaction.
Learning only the **breakdown** half of spec point 1.12 and forgetting that enzymes also catalyse **synthesis**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer never gives the same explanation twice for different causes. Asked why the rate is low at 5 °C **and** at 70 °C, it gives **fewer collisions from lower kinetic energy, reversible** for one and **denaturing, permanent** for the other, and says which is which. Its denaturing answer is a chain — bonds break, the **active site** changes shape, the substrate is no longer **complementary**, no complex forms — rather than a single word. Shown a saturated graph it says the limit is **active sites** and that **more enzyme**, not more substrate, would raise the rate. And it converts times to **rates** before comparing them, then uses the fact that doubling the time must halve the rate as a check.
